title: Draft budget bill proposes sweeping new land-seizure powers for high-speed rail | CBC News
html:
Politics·New

Draft budget bill proposes sweeping new land-seizure powers for high-speed rail

Planned changes would strip away standard expropriation and regulatory protections for Alto project

The federal government is proposing to scrap standard expropriation rules for Canada's first high-speed rail project.

If passed in the government's planned Budget 2026 implementation legislation, Ottawa could expropriate land without public hearings, transfer ownership directly to a private consortium and send unresolved crossing disputes for split farms and municipal roads to private arbitration.

In the draft legislation, the government hopes to give Alto bespoke powers around expropriation — including exempting Alto from the rules under the Railway Relocation and Crossing Act, key sections of the Railway Safety Act and Impact Assessment Act and the entirety of the Expropriation Act.

The Alto project proposes building a high-speed train between Toronto and Quebec City, and has been facing backlash from farmers, landowners and some municipal governments.

The current projected path for the Alto high-speed rail line that would connect Toronto to Quebec City. (Alto)

Alto declined to comment on the proposed legislation.

"Both in terms of dollar value and the number of private properties required, in my view, it will be the largest expropriation project in modern Canadian history," said municipal and land use planning lawyer Ajay Gajaria.

Gajaria says the proposed changes would give the government extraordinary powers to force landowners to sell, potentially affecting thousands of properties.

In the past, Ottawa could only seize private land for the Crown, and only after following strict rules and independent public hearings.

This 3D rendering shows what an Alto high-speed train could look like. (Alto)

When Parliament passed the High-Speed Rail Network Act as part of Bill C-15 in March, it carved out targeted exceptions to speed things up — allowing Alto to skip upfront purchase negotiations and replace public hearings with written objections, while still keeping the project anchored inside Canada's Expropriation Act.

This draft legislation would scrap remaining oversight and lets Ottawa seize private property and sign the deed to a third party.

The changes are laid out in a 521-page notice of ways and means motion posted on Nov. 20.

Right of first refusal

Gajaria said the parts that trouble him most are a carve-out where the government can lock down property rights for up to eight years and issue a prohibition on work for four years — before deciding whether it wants to expropriate the land at all.

Parts of this were included in C-15. The expanded powers proposed now are that the minister's discretion is expanded to consider "any factor … including the public interest" before registering a work ban.

"The right of first refusal and the prohibition on work, if used broadly, in my view, would go too far," Gajaria said.

Combined with powers passed in March, Alto would have the first chance for years to buy a target property — without needing to put cash up front.

"Somebody looking to purchase your property is going to see the presence of a right of first refusal for the Crown to essentially match the best offer," Gajaria said.

Those in the identified corridor, Gajaria said, "may have a circumstance where you cannot market or sell your property potentially for eight years, potentially longer."

The "notice of prohibition on work" can be issued on a target property for four years — meaning the landowner is legally banned from building anything new, putting on a major addition, digging or making significant improvements to the land or home without getting special permission from the transport minister.

The proposed legislation says any increase in property value from upgrades or work done in that period is legally excluded from the expropriation payout.

A sign with the word 'Alto' crossed out is shown along the road in Chaffey's Lock, Ont., in May 2026. (Dan Taekema/CBC)

Another change to the expropriation regulations is around the way a notice of expropriation is explained.

In the past, if a government expropriation notice to a landowner didn't clearly spell out exactly what portion of a property it was taking, the owner could have it thrown out in court. In March, Ottawa changed the rules to let officials fix defective notices and backdate the corrections to the original filing date.

This new motion goes a step further: if an expropriation notice leaves out what specific land is being taken, it automatically seizes 100 per cent of the owner's property rights and wipes out any existing easements, leases or rights-of-way.

"You likely will get compensated," Gajaria said of those who ultimately do get their land expropriated.

"The intent is that a person who is expropriated for a public project gets full and fair compensation for the property."

Farmers and crossing rights

Under traditional Canadian rail law, a farmer had a legal right to demand a crossing when a freight train cut across a farm or a rural road, and the Canadian Transportation Agency could order the railway to build and pay for what's known as a level crossing.

But when it comes to high-speed rail, where trains can reach speeds up to 300 km/h, the safety standards change.

Those crossings are required to be grade-separated — meaning the entire corridor needs to be sectioned off and every crossing has to be a concrete overpass or underpass.

Alto says it does not want to divide or separate communities, and that it does not intend to sever federal or provincial highways — building overpasses and underpasses when possible. (Alto)

For any private farm or town that has severed land, the proposed budget legislation forces the parties into private arbitration where they must split the costs — up to $25,000 per party, on top of their own legal fees. It would also let arbitrators bill landowners for part of building or maintaining a crossing.

"For costs to be apportioned on a 50/50 basis and costing up to $25,000 for an individual landowner," Gajaria said, "I do think that provision goes too far."

$24.5B in projected benefits annually

A recent study commissioned by Alto says that the rail line will boost productivity by better connecting people living and working in the Toronto-Quebec City corridor — and says once up and running, the line could generate around $24.5 billion worth of economic benefits annually.

The federal government has reiterated the importance of a project like Alto in Canada. It calls Alto a "bold step to address [Canada's] growing transportation needs" and part of a national "transformative strategy" designed to begin construction years ahead of schedule.

The Conservative Party and Bloc Québécois have come out against the Alto project, pointing to the planned expropriations as a major reason for their opposition.

The NDP supports high-speed rail development in Canada, but has reservations over the sweeping powers the Carney government is proposing.

"With high-speed rail, you don't have the latitude to go around things ... So sometimes expropriation is necessary, but that's the last resort," said NDP Leader Avi Lewis.

"Some of it's going to be public land, some of it's gonna be private land ... but we need these projects. It's a vast country."
summary: The federal government is proposing to scrap standard expropriation rules for Canada's first high-speed rail project.
